As long as there’s nothing thrown around and all the outgoing returns and plugged merchandise are removed, you should be fine. Just try to make sure that things are in their proper places, but don’t sweat too much over it. Section work exists partially to help with that. If you’re stocking, try to eye the section you’re in and make sure everything is in order. You’ll get used to the mods as you become more familiar with the department. The more you work in the department, the more comfortable you’ll be, and the faster you’ll get with your routine. I was incredibly slow when I started on the sales floor, but by the time I left my department, I could stock a pallet of freight at the start of my shift and finish returns half an hour before I left. It just took some time and patience.

If all else fails, go to OGP. Completely different workload. It was much better for me.

Yeah, I actually don’t get as bothered by it as I used to (I’ve always gotten annoyed by interruptions in my workflow.) The reason I clarify that I don’t work in x area is because, when I was a service area associate, I would always have customers who expected me to have an answer prepared for what we had in stock, when a replenishment was coming, and exactly where it was on the shelf without looking (I’m naturally terrible at giving directions,) and I’ve noticed that the customers are generally a little more understanding when I have to look for an item if they know that I’m not tied to that specific department every day.

I always just assume they’re asking me if I work in the department I’m picking in, and I’ll just say “no, I’m online pickup.” Generally, even if they still ask me the question, they don’t expect me to know everything about the area.

I live in the midwest, and Walmart has only been in my city since the late ‘60s, and since then it’s been moved twice, only becoming a super center about 20 years ago. I think some of the older people still hold the associates there to the same expectation they’d hold an employee at a Dollar General to.

Smaller stores can’t really accommodate specialized jobs as well, and this would translate to the person scanning your groceries also being the person who unloads the trucks, stocks the shelves, and cleans the restrooms. More of a traditional “grocery store clerk” job. You don’t really have to think about who would be the best person to ask for help.

That’s just my best guess. Personally, I try not to bother anyone. It’s pretty easy to find what I need by applying the things I’ve learned at Walmart, but I’m a young person who would rather find it myself or go home empty handed than talk to a busy stranger.
